title: Buffett & Munger Unscripted - A great book | Mohnish Pabrai discusses at SumZero

summary: The interview argues that investors should distinguish between companies with exceptional, entrenched management and those facing existential threats or speculative risks. The speaker advocates for a 'set it and forget it' approach to owning great businesses with concentrated ownership, such as Walmart and Microsoft, even at higher valuations, while avoiding companies where leadership distraction or regulatory threats undermine their moat. Conversely, the speaker expresses skepticism toward businesses like Tesla and Google where the lack of a singular visionary leader or core business challenges make the investment speculative or difficult to hold.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Bill Gates expressed concern that Apple is a 'weird company' heavily concentrated in a few products and lacks a leader like Steve Jobs to guide it to the next paradigm.
claims.quote: So when I mentioned when I mentioned Apple, his reaction was that and you know this is a guy who used to be in Burkshire's board and you know he's with Warren and all of that. So he said, well, you know, that's a very weird company. And what he was basically saying is it's all so heavily concentrated in these few products, right? I mean, if you really think about it, I mean, what Open AI is trying to do with Johnny IV coming in, right? Is take the brick out of our hands, right? So if you take the brick out of our hands, where is Apple? And I mean that's where they what they're trying to push towards is you can't make a better brick, you just need to take the brick out, right? And it's weird to go around with a brick actually, even though it's a nice slim brick, but it's weird to go around. So it somehow needs to get integrated into us. Well, that's why spending billions on glasses and other wearable tech. Uh so if we ever get down that path where the brick gets threatened then you have a problem right Apple has a problem then because they don't have Steve leading them to take them to the next paradigm. I have a concern whether Apple can get to the next paradigm.

claims.claim: Berkshire is viewed as a better index to invest in than the S&P 500 due to its large cash position, modest valuation, and relatively young leader.
claims.quote: But I think today it's actually a better index to invest in than the S&P. You know, in the past, like I said, like you mentioned, I've thought of it as a placeholder, but actually it's a better vehicle. I mean, now we have passive investing is more than half of all investing in the US. And one of the negatives with passive investing, we still don't see the extreme impacts of that is that you get this lemming behavior where a few stocks, you know, get money allocated to them regardless of fundamentals because they're in the index. And so that's why we see some of this MAG 7 stuff and all of that going on. But yeah, I mean, I think given Burkshire's large cash position, modest valuation, relatively young leader, it's a good place to be.
claims.speaker: Monish Pabrai

claims.claim: Google faces real challenges in its core business, specifically search being threatened, so the low multiple is not a strong signal to buy.
claims.quote: I would say this that company like Google faces real challenges in its core business. Now they've got you know I if you look at something like the YouTube franchise I mean that's just so spectacularly mind-blowing that you know it's it's a lot it's a rock not going anywhere. And of course, Android also is great, but I'm just saying that search search is threatened in a way that it wasn't threatened a few years ago. And Google has woken up to this. They're fully focused on it. They'll probably come out okay, but it's not the cinch that it was a few years back. So, to me, the Google multiple being low isn't really a strong signal that one should go out and buy the stock.
claims.speaker: Monish Pabrai

claims.claim: Microsoft is considered the closest to bulletproof due to deep enterprise entrenchment and exceptional leadership, despite a higher multiple.
claims.quote: The one that I really think is, you know, as close to bulletproof as you can get is Microsoft. I think because Microsoft is so embedded in the enterprise and because enterprises are like aircraft carriers, they cannot, you know, turn on a dime. They can't suddenly say, "Oh, I'm going to use someone else for search tomorrow." You know, we can make a decision 5 minutes from now to never use Google search and not even think about it again. But you can't do that with a lot of Microsoft products. Those are just so deeply entrenched and embedded and Satya is such an exceptional leader. And so to me, of course, Microsoft the multiple is higher.
claims.speaker: Monish Pabrai

claims.claim: Investing in Tesla is difficult and would veer towards speculation due to Elon Musk getting distracted by other things like running the government.
claims.quote: I mean from my point of view, it's difficult to invest in something like Tesla, especially difficult to invest in something like Tesla in anything resembling a 10% or bigger bet in my portfolio. It would kind of veer towards a speculator since simply because Elon gets distracted. You know, he goes and runs the government for a while and he's got so many things going on. But probably a mistake on my part. I think that not being long Elon is probably a mistake but you know we've made a lot of mistakes like that.
claims.speaker: Monish Pabrai

claims.claim: The speaker expresses regret for not buying Microsoft early and suggests holding great businesses even if they appear overpriced.
claims.quote: like I wish I had bought Microsoft when I was uh you know a pre-teen using you know Windows operating system back when there used to be like a 386 processor you know made by Intel and that could have been my one position and I'd be, you know, very wealthy just from that one, you know, trade alone.

claims.claim: The speaker advises keeping great businesses that are firing on all cylinders until they become egregiously overpriced.
claims.quote: And when you find yourself in the happy position of a partial ownership of one of those types of businesses, don't get cute by selling when you think it's overpriced or fully priced because you really don't know what that is. And so until it gets crazily egregiously overpriced and it's obvious that that's the case, if it's a great business that's still firing on all cylinders, just keep it.

claims.claim: The speaker views Noble as a valuable company with a tight market and great assets, noting it would print cash if rates increased.
claims.quote: So basically you cannot go out and build a ship today and every day and every year ships get scrapped and so this market is coming into a tightness. The other thing that people don't realize is that offshore drilling for oil has a very low cost. So like for example in Brazil which has huge amounts of offshore drilling their cost of producing oil is $ 20 to $30 a barrel.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Valaris has a tight market, great assets, low debt, and would generate massive cash flow if day rates increased.
claims.quote: And if rates were to go for example from the 400s to 6 or 700 a day, I mean Valeris and Noble, I mean they would be just printing almost the entire market cap in cash every year. So that's why Monish is there.

claims.claim: The speaker views TAV airports as a wonderful company with operating leverage where cash flows explode as passenger traffic grows.
claims.quote: And so, Tab Airports actually is a wonderful company because it has operating leverage. When passenger traffic goes up 5% or 10% in a year, their costs don't go up. It's pure operating leverage and so over time their cash flows are just exploding. Beautiful, beautiful business.
claims.speaker: Monish

claims.claim: The speaker previously owned the company but sold because the government threatened to destroy its monopoly, making it difficult to hold.
claims.quote: We used to own IEX. We don't own it anymore because there in the middle there was a lot of rumbling that started happening that the government was going to destroy that monopoly. It became very hard for us. We went in the too hard pile.
claims.speaker: Monish

claims.claim: The speaker cites the Walton family's long-term ownership and successful 'set it and forget it' management as evidence of Walmart's strength.
claims.quote: If we look at the Walton family and Walmart for example when Walmart went public you know 55 years ago the Walton family owned about 46% of Walmart. And if you look at it today they own 46% of Walmart. Okay. And I mean Sam Walton died 33 years ago and the founder passing away and leaders changing and all of that. They haven't done anything. They've been running this thing the way Balmer does, you know, set it and forget it, right?
claims.speaker: Monish

claims.claim: The speaker views Walmart as a highly successful, undervalued business with a 'set it and forget it' management style that has generated significant dividends and retained ownership concentration.
claims.quote: when we buy something at 2% of liquidation value in Turkey like we did and goes up, it's going to become like, you know, 40 50% of the portfolio and we're not going to trim that because it's still undervalued
